title: Application-scale fault-tolerant quantum computation

concept.text: The innovation would be a programmable quantum computer that keeps errors under control throughout a large, useful computation. It would combine many imperfect physical qubits into protected logical qubits, perform a universal set of logical operations, and run an application whose scale and reliability make it consequential—for example, cryptographic-size integer factoring or a scientifically useful quantum simulation with a persuasive advantage over classical methods.

Fault-tolerance theorems explain how reliable quantum computation can be possible under specified noise, locality, and architectural assumptions when physical errors are sufficiently weak. Turning that possibility into a machine requires more than preserving a quantum state: error correction, logical gates, decoding, classical control, and application execution must work together for the full computation. Protected memories and small logical circuits are milestones within this concept, rather than separate realizations of the application-scale goal.

significance.text: A successful machine would add a major computational capability to the existing digital-computing toolkit. Shor’s algorithms establish polynomial-time quantum methods for integer factoring and specified discrete-logarithm problems. Executing these methods at cryptographically relevant sizes would threaten RSA and other public-key cryptosystems whose security depends on the affected mathematical problems, wherever those systems remained deployed without adequate post-quantum protection. This is a concrete algorithmic consequence; it does not depend on quantum computers accelerating every kind of computation.

Quantum simulation offers another consequential application, particularly for selected quantum dynamics that are difficult to reproduce classically. Reliable application-scale computation could make some otherwise inaccessible physical predictions practical. Drug, battery, and materials discovery are conditional downstream possibilities: they additionally require suitable algorithms, tractable state preparation, informative measurements, relevant chemical models, and experimental validation. Neither universal programmability nor error correction establishes efficient solutions for every quantum-system problem, including difficult ground-state problems.

General logistics optimization and efficient solutions to NP-complete problems do not follow from this capability. Grover’s algorithm provides a quadratic improvement in exhaustive search, which can still leave an exponentially growing workload. The supplied perspective describes continuing uncertainty about useful quantum optimization advantages and does not establish polynomial-time quantum algorithms for NP-complete problems. These limits matter when translating a specific quantum advantage into claims about broad economic impact.

Interpretive synthesis: a checked application-scale quantum advantage would provide empirical evidence that quantum hardware can outperform practical classical competitors on a consequential task. A finite demonstration would not prove an asymptotic separation from every possible classical algorithm or a general impossibility of efficient classical simulation. Computation beyond the quantum model would require a separate physical and computational justification; it is not a consequence of fault tolerance.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is sustained, universal logical computation at an application scale, with a sufficiently low total failure probability and acceptable resource cost. A memory experiment tests whether encoded information survives. An application also requires reliable operations on that information, including the ingredients needed beyond Clifford circuits, while repeated measurements, decoding, and control continue throughout the run. Quantinuum’s supplied report identifies magic-state preparation and integrated real-time decoding among the remaining steps toward universal circuits.

The engineering challenge is to preserve error suppression as the machine grows and performs a much larger workload. Physical noise must remain compatible with the assumptions underlying the chosen code and architecture; logical gates must be protected alongside storage; and classical decoding and control must respond quickly enough to support the computation. A low error rate in a small code or an offline decoding analysis does not by itself establish these capabilities in an integrated machine.

Resource overhead remains a concrete barrier. Physical qubits are the noisy hardware elements; logical qubits are the protected computational units built from them. Gidney’s RSA-2048 estimate concerns fewer than one million noisy physical qubits, not millions of logical qubits. Its feasibility depends on hardware timing, connectivity, noise, algorithmic choices, and storage behavior. Achieving an attractive projected qubit count therefore requires realizing the model’s operating assumptions, rather than merely manufacturing that number of qubits.

Useful application execution also requires credible validation and classical comparison. Factoring has an easily checked output because the proposed factors can be multiplied. A large quantum simulation can be harder to verify: agreement with experiments, known limits, or smaller exactly solvable cases contributes evidence, but does not alone certify an answer in a larger classically inaccessible regime. Application value depends on the complete preparation, computation, measurement, and validation process, alongside the strength of competing classical methods.

current_state.text: Eisert and Preskill’s assessment, first submitted in October 2025 and revised on 21 May 2026, describes substantial gaps between noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices and application-scale fault-tolerant machines. It distinguishes extended quantum memories from the subsequent realization of universal computers that solve hard problems. The demonstrations covered by the supplied review do not establish cryptographic-size Shor execution or a universal application-scale machine. Because the supplied freshness record is empty, this is a conclusion about the reviewed sources, not an exhaustive survey through 1 November 2026.

Google’s Willow experiment, published online on 9 December 2024 and appearing in Nature in 2025, reports a 101-qubit distance-7 surface-code memory with an error rate of 0.143% ± 0.003 percentage points per correction cycle and a lifetime beyond breakeven. Integrated real-time decoding was demonstrated separately at distance 5; it should not be attributed to the distance-7 result. The retrieved main article records an author correction dated 28 April 2026. The supplied review did not inspect the separate correction text or establish its precise effects, so these figures retain that qualification. Supplementary artifacts in the source index do not extend the review’s stated inspection scope.

Quantinuum’s Helios preprint, submitted on 16 October 2026, reports color-code memories at distances 3, 5, and 7, together with below-threshold two-qubit Clifford benchmarking at distances 3 and 5. Its estimated distance-7 memory error rate is approximately 5×10^-6 per syndrome-extraction cycle, with a reported interval of 3×10^-6 to 9×10^-6. The estimate comes from three failures in 29,000 shots, each lasting 20 cycles, making the finite-shot uncertainty important to interpretation. This is a preprint report of small encoded memories and circuits, rather than an application-scale universal computation.

All decoding in the Quantinuum experiment was performed offline. Decoder timing studies indicate potential for real-time integration, but do not constitute an integrated real-time demonstration. Its memory error rate and Google’s rate also come from different codes and experimental protocols; the supplied review does not establish a controlled comparison between the platforms. The results demonstrate progress in error correction without resolving the remaining universal-gate, control, and application-scaling requirements.

Gidney’s May 2025 analysis estimates RSA-2048 factoring in under a week with fewer than one million noisy physical qubits; the reviewed resource accounting gives a total of 897,864 physical qubits. This is a planning estimate, not a hardware demonstration. It assumes a square nearest-neighbor grid, uniform 0.1% gate errors, a 1-microsecond surface-code cycle, and a 10-microsecond control reaction time, alongside algorithmic and implementation assumptions. The review also identifies conjectural algorithmic assumptions and unfinished detailed analysis and simulation of cold-storage behavior under different workloads. The numerical estimate must be interpreted within those conditions.

The historical threshold theorem supplies a foundation for these efforts rather than evidence of a completed machine. The supplied review inspected its opening discussion of locality and reliable universal computation, but the retained PDF extraction is truncated on page 39. That limitation does not negate the supported theorem-to-machine distinction; it limits claims about coverage of the complete technical treatment.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed sufficient cryptanalytic milestone: factor an independently selected public RSA modulus of at least 2048 bits, constructed from two comparably sized primes, with its factors unavailable to the implementers beforehand. Use Shor’s algorithm or an equivalent peer-reviewed quantum cryptanalytic algorithm, execute fault-tolerant logical operations with ongoing error correction, and verify the factors classically. A circuit whose construction already uses the factors would not qualify. The 2048-bit threshold is a proposed criterion for this record, not an established consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Classically verified fault-tolerant factoring of unknown ≥2048-bit RSA modulus

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidence requirements: publish the computation protocol, circuit-generation procedure, physical and logical resource counts, decoding and control methods, run records, success statistics, and end-to-end elapsed time. Compare the result with credible classical methods on the same task, including relevant preparation and processing costs. Make enough information available for independent scrutiny and replication, and repeat the demonstration on independently selected inputs so that a single favorable instance does not carry the whole claim.
completion_criteria.label: Published records and independent replications versus credible classical methods

completion_criteria.text: Proposed universality requirement: establish programmable execution of a universal logical gate set separately from the factoring result, including the operations beyond the demonstrated Clifford circuits and their integration with real-time correction and control. Protected memory, sampling, or one specialized application alone would not establish unrestricted programmability. Finite tests could demonstrate a stated breadth of programs, scales, and operating conditions; they could not establish literal universality by exhaustive testing.
completion_criteria.label: Programmable universal logical gates beyond Clifford with real-time correction

completion_criteria.text: Proposed alternative application milestone: execute a scientifically useful quantum simulation at a scale where the complete computation offers a persuasive accuracy or time advantage over strong classical methods. Specify the physical question, error tolerance, state-preparation and measurement costs, and a validation strategy suitable for the otherwise inaccessible regime. Smaller exact cases and experimental agreement should contribute to that strategy without being presented as complete verification of the larger answer. This preserves the broader concept rather than making cryptanalysis its exclusive completion route.
completion_criteria.label: Useful quantum simulation with persuasive advantage over strong classical methods

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: report the demonstrated workload size, runtime, failure probability, calibration demands, and hardware and classical-computing requirements. A convincing application-scale demonstration need not establish commercial value in every domain or efficient solutions to arbitrary computational problems. Its claim should remain bounded by the applications and operating conditions actually demonstrated.
completion_criteria.label: Reported practical bounds on workload, reliability, and computing requirements

related_concepts.text: CSC-01, Practical polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems, concerns a different computational breakthrough. Application-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing would implement known quantum capabilities, while Grover’s quadratic search advantage does not supply polynomial-time solutions to NP-complete problems. The roster provides CSC-01’s title but no detailed definition, so a more specific boundary cannot be assessed.

Roster-based synthesis: CSC-05, Routine-cost general computation on encrypted data, and CSC-09, Practical indistinguishability obfuscation, share a cryptographic context with this entry but concern different capabilities. They address computation while protecting information or program details; this entry concerns reliable execution of quantum algorithms, including algorithms that threaten particular cryptographic assumptions. The supplied titles do not establish that either privacy technology is automatically defeated or enabled by this machine.

Roster-based synthesis: CSC-04, Industrial-cost proof-carrying software; CSC-07, Reliable machine-checked mathematical discovery; and CSC-10, Machine-checked behavioral guarantees for frontier learned models, overlap with the demand for trustworthy computational results. Their central goals concern proofs, discovery, or behavioral guarantees. Fault-tolerant quantum computation instead protects a physical computation against errors. Classical verification of factors is useful evidence for a quantum run, but it does not itself deliver any of those broader verification capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: CSC-03, Competent general machine intelligence; CSC-06, A predictive theory of generalization for modern learning systems; and CSC-08, General-purpose physical autonomy in unmodified environments, concern intelligence, learning theory, and embodied action. Quantum hardware might eventually serve particular subroutines within such systems, but the supplied material establishes no dependency or automatic route from quantum fault tolerance to these outcomes. They remain distinct entries.

change_log.change: Preserved CSC-02’s identity and broad application-scale scope, with protected memory, logical gates, decoding, and application execution treated as components of one capability.
change_log.reason: The review supports a coherent enabling technology and distinguishes intermediate demonstrations from completion.

change_log.change: Expanded the threshold-theorem explanation to include noise, locality, and architectural assumptions.
change_log.reason: A constant error threshold is conditional and does not by itself establish a practical machine.

change_log.change: Separated application validation from agreement with smaller exact cases or chemistry experiments.
change_log.reason: Such agreement contributes evidence but does not alone certify a larger classically inaccessible simulation.

change_log.change: Corrected resource accounting to noisy physical qubits and retained the reviewed total of 897,864 in Gidney’s model.
change_log.reason: The headline estimate does not describe millions of logical qubits or completed hardware.

change_log.change: Added the square-grid and 10-microsecond control-reaction assumptions, conjectural algorithmic assumptions, and unfinished cold-storage workload analysis to the resource estimate.
change_log.reason: These conditions materially affect interpretation of the projected qubit count and runtime.

change_log.change: Separated Google’s distance-7 memory result from its distance-5 integrated real-time decoding demonstration and retained the correction-text limitation.
change_log.reason: The supplied review supports those distinct achievements but did not inspect the separate author correction.

change_log.change: Expanded Quantinuum’s preprint result with per-cycle normalization, the reported uncertainty interval, finite-shot counts, Clifford benchmarking distances, and offline decoding.
change_log.reason: These details define the scope and evidential strength of the reported achievement.

change_log.change: Replaced an unbounded claim that no application-scale machine was found with a conclusion limited to the reviewed sources.
change_log.reason: The empty freshness record cannot establish exhaustive coverage through 1 November 2026.

change_log.change: Retained the conditional cryptanalytic and simulation significance while removing the precise random-oracle bound and elliptic-curve-specific attribution from the substantive claims.
change_log.reason: The former lacks a retained source artifact, and the inspected Shor paper does not specifically establish the latter extension. Neither limitation undermines the central concept.

change_log.change: Distinguished empirical quantum advantage from a proof of asymptotic classical impossibility and qualified broad simulation and optimization claims.
change_log.reason: Finite demonstrations and known quantum algorithms do not establish unrestricted computational superiority.

change_log.change: Strengthened the proposed RSA milestone against pre-solved inputs, added replication and classical comparisons, and separated universal programmability from one application.
change_log.reason: A convincing application demonstration must exclude encoded solutions and should not overstate what one successful algorithm establishes.

change_log.change: Added an explicit simulation completion route and kept all proposed thresholds and evidence requirements labeled as proposals.
change_log.reason: Cryptanalysis is a sufficient proposed milestone, not the exclusive definition of this broader innovation or a published consensus standard.

change_log.change: Used the supplied roster titles to explain relevant relationships across the remaining entries, with title-based inferences labeled as synthesis.
change_log.reason: The roster supplies identities but not full definitions; the relationships should not imply unsupported dependencies or merge distinct concepts.

unresolved_issues: The supplied freshness record is empty, so comprehensive coverage through 1 November 2026 remains unestablished.
The separate Google author correction dated 28 April 2026 was not inspected in the supplied review; its precise changes and any effects on the stated results remain unresolved.
Quantinuum’s October 2026 findings are preprint reports in this packet. Independent replication and subsequent peer-reviewed disposition are not established here.

The precise Bennett–Bernstein–Brassard–Vazirani random-oracle lower bound cannot be verified from the packet because the cited zbMATH source has no retained artifact. Its omission is an evidence limitation, not a finding that the theorem is false.
The original elliptic-curve-specific cryptanalytic assertion is not established by the inspected Shor paper; resolving that attribution would require evidence outside this packet.
Gidney’s estimate retains conjectural algorithmic assumptions and unfinished cold-storage workload analysis; the packet does not resolve their effect on realizable resources and runtime.
A concrete validation protocol for a classically inaccessible application-scale simulation remains application dependent and is not specified by the supplied sources.
Related-concept boundaries beyond the supplied roster titles remain provisional because full definitions of the other entries were not provided.

The research mentions Preskill’s February 2025 Megaquop perspective, but the supplied source index and validated review do not document its inspection. Its historical statement about commercially valuable NISQ advantage was not promoted into an independently reviewed current-state claim.
